jsnvu6-e182717-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 3 of d.24: whether reasons adduced for matters of faith diminish the merit of faith, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e117.summary: Argument that reasons diminish merit: contraries have contrary effects, and what opposes faith—persecution or contrary arguments—increases merit, so reasons supporting faith diminish it.
claims: Reasons supporting faith diminish merit, since opposition increases it (objection)

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e135.summary: Second argument: as an efficacious proof would wholly remove faith's merit—Gregory: faith has no merit where human reason provides proof—so a merely persuasive reason diminishes it proportionally.
claims: Demonstration removes merit, so persuasion diminishes it (objection from Gregory)

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e156.summary: Argument for the opposite: eternal life is promised to those who elucidate faith (Sirach 24), and reasons concordant with faith elucidate it.
claims: Elucidating faith by reasons merits reward

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e172.summary: Second argument for the opposite: 1 Peter 3 exhorts us always to be ready to give a reason for the faith and hope in us, which Peter would not do if it diminished merit.
claims: Giving reasons for the faith is exhorted, so it does not diminish merit

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e183.summary: Outline: first, whether believing what is above reason is meritorious; second, whether reasons for or against diminish merit. These do not conflict, since matters of faith, though beyond demonstrative or fully efficacious reasoning, can be clarified by probable arguments.
claims: Articles of faith are above demonstrative reason but can be clarified by probable arguments

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e205.summary: First article: given charity and the wayfarer's state, merit also requires that the act be in our power and that it be good (venial sin does not merit even in one with charity). Believing is in our power: everyone experiences that he believes freely and could not believe, and not all have faith (2 Thess. 3).
claims: Merit requires charity, the state of via, a free act, and a good act
Believing is a free act, as experience shows

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e231.summary: Whether believing what is entirely above reason is a good act: one might think abandoning reason, our noblest part, is blameworthy. But faith never wholly abandons reason, since the middle of believing resolves to something reason concurs with, generally and specially. Generally, reason itself dictates that we cannot comprehend God or his works by our own power and so ought to assent on the authority of God who knows them.
claims: Faith never wholly abandons reason
Reason itself dictates assent to God's authority about what exceeds it

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e277.summary: Specially, the final credible to which all resolve—that the Church does not err in faith, directed by the Holy Spirit (Luke 22: 'that your faith may not fail')—is supported by reason from appearances: a doctrine confirmed by so many signs and preserved by martyrs through torment is true. Indeed meritorious belief is impossible otherwise: assent requires that something appear true, either in itself or through a middle, and to avoid infinite regress there must be a first appearing true in itself. So faith presupposes reason, though not demonstration; thus Christ referred his teaching to miracles (John 10), and the apostles' preaching was confirmed by signs (Mark 16). Believing is therefore meritorious, being free, good, and concordant with reason.
claims: The final credible, the Church's inerrancy, is supported by reason from signs and martyrdom
Assent requires something ultimately apparent as true in itself
Faith presupposes non-demonstrative reason
Belief with charity is meritorious as free, good, and concordant with reason

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e348.summary: Second article: merit increases or decreases on the side of the work (by goodness and difficulty) and on the side of the agent (by voluntariness). A reason against faith adds difficulty and, with will unchanged, increases merit. A reason for faith either precedes or follows faith. Preceding: if demonstrative it removes merit, by imposing necessity and making faith unnecessary, though no demonstration is possible for proper articles like the Trinity or Incarnation; if probable, it neither removes merit (being in fact required for assent) nor diminishes it, since it gives no evidence and so does not reduce the act's difficulty, while increasing voluntariness. Following: demonstration voids subsequent merit of assent, though the disposition to believe without it remains meritorious; probable reasons do not diminish merit, and reasoning out of love of faith signals greater will and greater merit.
claims: Merit varies by the work's goodness and difficulty and by the agent's voluntariness
Reasons against faith increase merit if belief remains firm
Demonstration removes the merit of assent by imposing necessity
Proper articles of faith cannot be demonstrated
Probable reasons for faith neither remove nor diminish merit and may increase it

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e442.summary: Reply to the first argument: contrary and concordant reasons tend to contrary effects regarding faith itself—corrupting or confirming it—but not regarding merit: a contrary reason adds difficulty and so increases merit if belief stays firm, while a probable concordant reason does not decrease difficulty and increases the will's readiness, so it does not diminish merit and rather increases it.
claims: Contrary and concordant reasons do not affect merit in contrary ways

jsnvu6-e182717-d1e477.summary: Reply to the second: demonstration and persuasion are not proportional in their effect on merit; demonstration removes all difficulty and imposes necessity incompatible with merit, whereas persuasion removes neither difficulty, freedom, nor readiness of will, and so does not diminish merit.
claims: Persuasive reasons are not a lesser degree of demonstration regarding merit

jsnvu6-e182717.summary: Question 3 of d.24 asks whether reasons adduced for matters of faith diminish its merit. First, believing what is above reason is meritorious, given charity and the state of the wayfarer. Belief is free, as experience shows, and it is good, because faith never wholly abandons reason. In general, reason itself counsels assent to God's authority about what exceeds it. In particular, the final credible, the Church's inerrancy under the Spirit, is supported by reason from signs, miracles, and martyrdom. Assent requires something ultimately apparent as true, so faith presupposes non-demonstrative reason, as Christ referred his teaching to his works. Second, merit varies with the work's goodness and difficulty and with the agent's voluntariness. Reasons against faith increase merit if belief holds firm. Demonstrative reasons remove the merit of assent by imposing necessity, but they are impossible for proper articles. Probable reasons, whether before or after faith, give no evidence, leave difficulty and freedom intact, and increase readiness of will, so they do not diminish merit and, when sought out of love, signal greater merit.
claims: Belief in what is above reason is meritorious, being free, good, and concordant with reason
Faith presupposes non-demonstrative reason, ultimately grounded in signs confirming the Church's teaching
Demonstration removes the merit of assent; proper articles cannot be demonstrated
Probable reasons for faith do not diminish merit and may increase it
Reasons against faith increase merit when belief remains firm
